news_summary: Rural women in Kazakhstan are empowering themselves through collective initiatives to enhance their livelihoods, while Somalia advances toward stability as the UN's political mission concludes.
news_summary_fr: Au Kazakhstan, les femmes des zones rurales s'autonomisent grâce à des initiatives collectives visant à améliorer leurs moyens de subsistance, tandis qu'en Somalie, le pays s'achemine vers la stabilité alors que la mission politique de l'ONU touche à sa fin.
news_summary_es: Las mujeres de las zonas rurales de Kazajistán se están empoderando a través de iniciativas colectivas destinadas a mejorar sus medios de vida, mientras que Somalia avanza hacia la estabilidad a medida que concluye la misión política de la ONU.

articles.title: In Kazakhstan, rural women are forming collectives to improve their livelihoods
articles.summary: The planned cooperative would support joint advocacy, shared learning, and exploration of funding opportunities for smart-well or shared irrigation infrastructure.
articles.content:
This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Women in the rural areas of Kazakhstan are among those most affected by climate change, energy deficit, and poor governance. They bear the heavy burden of water shortages, especially in the southern parts of the country, where this problem is the most acute due to dense population, economic reliance on agriculture, and water losses related to outdated irrigation infrastructure.

In the village of Qyzylsay, located in the southern Jambyl region, the water shortage has become a major issue affecting the daily lives of women. It forces them to spend multiple hours a day outside their homes to secure water for their households, gardens, and animals. Their grueling work often goes unnoticed and unpaid, and their geographical remoteness places limits on access to information and government services, exacerbating their situation.

In 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, a local activist, implemented a project to help local women improve their livelihoods by training them to engage with the government more effectively and efficiently, calculate the cost of their labor and products, and mobilize collective efforts to solve community problems. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Aidabossynova to learn more about her initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Nazgul Aidabossynova (NA): I represent a community-based initiative led by rural women in Qyzylsay. Our work focuses on supporting women who manage households, small farms, livestock, and care responsibilities, while also facing limited access to information, public services, and opportunities for civic participation. We chose to participate in the Digital Sparks project because digital tools can make a direct, practical difference in women’s daily lives. Many women already own smartphones, but previously used them mainly for calls and WhatsApp. The project created an opportunity to turn these devices into tools for accessing eGov services, documenting community problems, managing farm and household responsibilities, protecting digital security, and communicating with local authorities.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

NA: The key challenge is unreliable access to water in Qyzylsay. Water often disappears from the pipes during the day, particularly in summer. This affects gardens, livestock, household work, and the health and well-being of families. The burden falls disproportionately on women. They wake early to store water, carry water for household and agricultural needs, care for the livestock, and wait for irrigation turns. Much of this work is unpaid, time-consuming, and rarely recognized. Women also faced barriers in reporting water problems: they knew what was happening, but often lacked the knowledge, evidence, and confidence needed to raise concerns effectively with local institutions.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

NA: The project delivered four practical training sessions for ten rural women. The first one, titled “Your Phone is More Than WhatsApp: Smartphone as Your Household Assistant”, taught them how to use smartphone reminders, photo-diaries for farm and livestock work, eGov services, strong passwords, and basic digital-security practices. In the second workshop, titled “Smart Water: When Your Garden Tells You It’s Thirsty”, participants learned about water rights, the responsibilities of relevant local authorities, and water-supply mapping using timestamped and GPS-tagged photographs. The third session, titled “Numbers Don’t Lie: When You Count Everything, You Earn More”, covered how to track unpaid work and calculate the real cost of agricultural products such as milk. It also discussed the economic value of time saved through smart irrigation. In “Honest Agreement: When Technology Helps Us Trust Each Other”, the fourth and final session, participants prepared time-to-income plans, mapped local support networks, discussed peer mentoring, and agreed to begin work toward a cooperative approach to water advocacy and shared smart-irrigation infrastructure.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

NA: The project helped participating women see smartphones as tools for independence, civic participation, and practical problem-solving, rather than only communication devices. For example, women learned that they can use eGov services to request certain official documents online, reducing the need to spend time and money traveling to administrative offices. They also learned to create structured evidence of water problems. A photograph of a dry canal, broken pipe, or contaminated water source becomes more useful for advocacy when it includes the date, location, and a written description. The training on unpaid labor and production costs was especially meaningful. Participants calculated the value of their time and better understood the real cost of milk production and irrigation work. The discussion showed that manual irrigation may take up to 60 hours per month. This helped participants recognize that their time has economic value, and that shared smart-irrigation solutions could create more time for income, education, rest, and community participation. The group also began a peer-learning process. Three participants started sharing the knowledge gained during the training with neighboring women.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

NA: My understanding of digital democracy has become much more practical. Before this project, digital tools could be viewed mainly as a way to communicate or access information. Through Digital Sparks, I saw how digital tools can strengthen people’s ability to exercise rights, access public services, collect evidence, engage with local authorities, and organize collectively. I also gained a stronger understanding of the link between digital inclusion, women’s unpaid labor, climate-related water challenges, and civic space. For rural women, digital capacity is not only about technical skills. It is about having a voice, being able to document problems, understanding their rights, and participating in decisions that affect their families and community.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

NA: The most valuable lesson is that digital literacy has the greatest impact when it is directly connected to people’s real, daily needs. In Qyzylsay, water shortages, agricultural work, unpaid care responsibilities, and access to public services were the issues that made digital tools relevant and useful. Another important lesson is that women need not only information, but also confidence and collective support. When participants understood their rights, calculated the value of their labor, and learned how to create reliable evidence, they became more prepared to speak with local authorities and work together. The project also showed the value of peer learning. Participants are more likely to trust and learn from women in their own community who face similar challenges.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

articles.personality_title: Rural women in Kazakhstan use digital tools to tackle water shortages
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In southern Kazakhstan, many rural women face serious problems because of climate change and old irrigation systems. Water shortages make their daily work harder, especially in farming and caring for animals. These women often spend many unpaid hours fetching water and have little access to government help or information.

**What happened** – In 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, a local activist from the village of Qyzylsay, started a project to help women use smartphones for more than just calls. Through four training sessions, women learned to use digital tools to track water problems, access government services online, calculate the value of their work, and plan for shared irrigation solutions. They also began forming a cooperative to improve water access together.

**Impact** – The project changed how women see their smartphones: as tools to support their rights and solve problems. They learned to gather clear evidence of water issues using photos with dates and locations, which helps when talking to local authorities. Understanding the real value of their unpaid work showed them that shared irrigation could save many hours each month. This knowledge gave them confidence and motivation to work as a group.

**What's next step** – The women plan to continue sharing what they learned with neighbors and develop their cooperative to advocate for better water infrastructure. They aim to use digital skills to keep improving their community’s access to water and public services.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Rural women in Kazakhstan are using digital tools and teamwork to overcome water shortages and improve their communities’ well-being.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des femmes rurales du Kazakhstan utilisent des outils numériques pour lutter contre la sécheresse
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dans le sud du Kazakhstan, de nombreuses femmes rurales rencontrent de graves problèmes à cause du changement climatique et des anciens systèmes d’irrigation. Le manque d’eau complique leur travail quotidien, notamment dans l’agriculture et le soin des animaux. Ces femmes passent souvent de nombreuses heures non rémunérées à chercher de l’eau et ont peu accès aux services gouvernementaux ou à l’information.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, une militante locale du village de Qyzylsay, a lancé un projet pour aider les femmes à utiliser leur smartphone autrement que pour téléphoner. Lors de quatre formations, elles ont appris à utiliser des outils numériques pour suivre les problèmes d’eau, accéder aux services publics en ligne, calculer la valeur de leur travail, et planifier des solutions d’irrigation partagée. Elles ont aussi commencé à former une coopérative pour améliorer ensemble l’accès à l’eau.

**Impact** – Le projet a changé la façon dont les femmes perçoivent leur smartphone : comme un outil pour défendre leurs droits et résoudre des problèmes. Elles ont appris à recueillir des preuves claires des problèmes d’eau grâce à des photos datées et géolocalisées, ce qui aide lors des discussions avec les autorités locales. Comprendre la vraie valeur de leur travail non rémunéré leur a montré que l’irrigation partagée pourrait leur faire économiser de nombreuses heures chaque mois. Cette connaissance leur a donné confiance et motivation pour agir en groupe.

**Prochaine étape** – Les femmes prévoient de continuer à partager leurs apprentissages avec leurs voisines et de développer leur coopérative pour défendre une meilleure infrastructure hydraulique. Elles veulent utiliser leurs compétences numériques pour continuer à améliorer l’accès à l’eau et aux services publics dans leur communauté.

**Une phrase clé** – Des femmes rurales du Kazakhstan utilisent les outils numériques et le travail collectif pour surmonter la pénurie d’eau et améliorer le bien-être de leur communauté.
articles.personality_title_es: Mujeres rurales en Kazajistán usan herramientas digitales para enfrentar la escasez de agua
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En el sur de Kazajistán, muchas mujeres rurales enfrentan serios problemas debido al cambio climático y a sistemas antiguos de riego. La escasez de agua dificulta su trabajo diario, especialmente en la agricultura y el cuidado de animales. Estas mujeres suelen pasar muchas horas no remuneradas buscando agua y tienen poco acceso a servicios gubernamentales o información.

**Qué pasó** – En 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, una activista local del pueblo Qyzylsay, inició un proyecto para ayudar a las mujeres a usar sus teléfonos inteligentes para más que solo llamadas. A través de cuatro sesiones de capacitación, aprendieron a usar herramientas digitales para registrar problemas de agua, acceder a servicios gubernamentales en línea, calcular el valor de su trabajo y planificar soluciones de riego compartido. También comenzaron a formar una cooperativa para mejorar juntas el acceso al agua.

**Impacto** – El proyecto cambió la forma en que las mujeres ven sus teléfonos: como herramientas para apoyar sus derechos y resolver problemas. Aprendieron a recopilar evidencia clara de los problemas de agua usando fotos con fechas y ubicaciones, lo que ayuda al hablar con las autoridades locales. Entender el valor real de su trabajo no remunerado les mostró que el riego compartido podría ahorrarles muchas horas al mes. Este conocimiento les dio confianza y motivación para trabajar en grupo.

**Próximo paso** – Las mujeres planean seguir compartiendo lo aprendido con sus vecinas y desarrollar su cooperativa para defender una mejor infraestructura de agua. Quieren usar sus habilidades digitales para seguir mejorando el acceso al agua y a los servicios públicos en su comunidad.

**Una frase clave** – Mujeres rurales en Kazajistán usan herramientas digitales y trabajo en equipo para superar la escasez de agua y mejorar el bienestar de sus comunidades.

articles.title: Somalia looks to the future as the UN's political mission closes
articles.summary: “The story of the UN's political engagement in Somalia has been one of persistence, partnership and adaptation,” Raisedon Zenenga, the UN Secretary-General's Deputy Special Representative for Somalia has said, as three decades of UN political missions in the Horn of Africa country comes to an end on 31 October.
articles.content:
The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia, known as UNTMIS, wraps up its work on Saturday and according to Mr. Zenenga “while significant challenges remain, the closure of UNTMIS comes after considerable progress by Somalia since the early years of international efforts to support the country's recovery.”

Somalia has undergone a profound transformation since the early 1990s, when the collapse of central State institutions and the outbreak of civil war ushered in years of conflict, instability and humanitarian crises.

UN Somalia/Adihamiid Mohamed

The conflict sparked a major outflow of refugees and internal displacements, while ongoing insecurity, contested electoral processes and constitutional reform, as well as recurrent climatic shocks – including droughts and floods – compounded humanitarian needs and presented formidable challenges to the country's recovery.

Somalia’s responsibility

Successive political missions accompanied Somalia through critical stages of its peacebuilding and State-building journey, supporting Somali-led efforts to restore governance, rebuild institutions and foster national reconciliation.

With the end of the UNTMIS, it is now Somali institutions which will take on the full responsibility for the country’s recovery with support from UN agencies already working in the country.

“Somalia today possesses national and federal institutions that did not exist when the UN’s political engagement began. Progress has been made in State formation, political inclusion, constitutional processes, human rights frameworks and the development of governance structures that enable Somali-led decision-making,” said Mr. Zenenga.

“However, continued engagement by the international community will remain important to sustaining progress and addressing outstanding priorities,” he added.

© WFP/Arete/Ahmed Luzako

Humanitarian and development support

That engagement includes some 25 UN entities that are still working across Somalia on humanitarian and development support.

In September, in the town of Balcad, a run-down vegetable market got a makeover from the UN's migration agency, IOM.

Tweet URL

There are now 56 sturdy stalls, running water and solar lighting. About 70 per cent of the stalls went to women-headed households, women-led businesses and small enterprises.

Elsewhere, Somalia's health ministry, working with UNICEF, launched national guidelines on caring for newborns, including babies who are small or sick.

In Puntland, where nearly a million children are out of school, the UN's food agency FAO is backing a school meals programme that links 1,330 local farmers and fisherfolk to schools serving 18,700 children, so kids eat and families earn.

And in Baidoa, mine action experts from UNMAS helped Somali authorities teach hundreds of students and teachers how to spot explosive dangers.

A complex crisis

The UN's humanitarian affairs office, OCHA, calls the situation in Somalia one of the world's most complex crises.

Conflict and climate shocks keep feeding each other, and families who fled drought or fighting have often been uprooted a second or third time by floods or fresh violence.

This year, 4.8 million Somalis, out of a population of just under 20 million, need humanitarian help.

Aid agencies are asking for $852 million to reach 2.4 million people, just half of those in need, and by mid-October only about 35 per cent of that had arrived.

The UN Secretary-General also wants continued support to tackle the threat from the terror group Al-Shabaab and to help Somalia move to a gradual, sustainable security transition.

© WFP/Arete/Abdirahman Yussuf Mohamud

Looking ahead, one huge challenge for Somalia's leaders after October is poverty.

They'll need to tackle it while steadying an economy that's still fragile. It leans heavily on subsistence farming, livestock, money sent home by relatives abroad and pastoralism.

The country imports more than 90 per cent of its essential goods, according to OCHA.

UN will remain

While UNTMIS is closing down, the United Nations is not leaving. UN humanitarian and development agencies continue to support Somalia and its people.

“Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia,” Deputy Special Representative Zenenga said. "It marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

It emphasizes the transition of responsibility to Somali institutions, ongoing international support for humanitarian and development aid, and programs benefiting vulnerable populations, which collectively represent a hopeful and inspiring development for Somalia's future stability and development.
articles.personality_title: UN closes political mission in Somalia after 30 years of support
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Somalia faced decades of conflict and instability starting in the early 1990s, after its central government collapsed. This led to civil war, many people fleeing their homes, and repeated crises like droughts and floods.

**What happened** – On October 31, the United Nations ended its political mission in Somalia, called UNTMIS, after nearly 30 years of helping the country rebuild. The UN’s Deputy Special Representative, Raisedon Zenenga, said this move comes as Somalia has made real progress in building government institutions and improving political processes.

**Impact** – The end of the UNTMIS mission means Somalia’s own government now fully leads its recovery efforts. Important improvements have been made in setting up national and regional governments, protecting human rights, and encouraging political participation. Meanwhile, UN agencies continue to help with health, education, food, and safety projects, such as new market stalls for women and school meal programs.

**What's next step** – Somalia faces challenges like poverty, a fragile economy, and security threats from groups like Al-Shabaab. The international community will keep supporting Somalia through humanitarian aid and development programs. Somali leaders will work on strengthening their economy and maintaining peace.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After decades of UN political support, Somalia is taking charge of its future while continuing to receive important international aid for lasting progress.
articles.personality_title_fr: L'ONU met fin à sa mission politique en Somalie après 30 ans d'appui
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La Somalie a connu des décennies de conflit et d'instabilité depuis le début des années 1990, après l'effondrement de son gouvernement central. Cela a entraîné une guerre civile, de nombreux déplacements de population et des crises répétées comme des sécheresses et des inondations.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Le 31 octobre, l'Organisation des Nations Unies a mis fin à sa mission politique en Somalie, appelée UNTMIS, après près de 30 ans d'aide au pays pour se reconstruire. Le représentant adjoint spécial de l'ONU, Raisedon Zenenga, a déclaré que cette décision survient alors que la Somalie a réalisé de réels progrès dans la construction d'institutions gouvernementales et l'amélioration des processus politiques.

**Impact** – La fin de la mission UNTMIS signifie que le gouvernement somalien dirige désormais pleinement ses efforts de reconstruction. Des améliorations importantes ont été faites dans la mise en place de gouvernements nationaux et régionaux, la protection des droits humains et la promotion de la participation politique. Parallèlement, les agences de l'ONU continuent d'aider avec des projets de santé, d'éducation, d'alimentation et de sécurité, comme de nouveaux marchés pour les femmes et des programmes de repas scolaires.

**Étape suivante** – La Somalie fait face à des défis comme la pauvreté, une économie fragile et des menaces sécuritaires de groupes comme Al-Shabaab. La communauté internationale continuera à soutenir la Somalie par l'aide humanitaire et les programmes de développement. Les dirigeants somaliens travailleront à renforcer leur économie et à maintenir la paix.

**En une phrase** – Après des décennies de soutien politique de l'ONU, la Somalie prend en main son avenir tout en continuant à recevoir une aide internationale importante pour un progrès durable.
articles.personality_title_es: La ONU cierra su misión política en Somalia tras 30 años de apoyo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Somalia enfrentó décadas de conflicto e inestabilidad desde principios de los años 90, tras el colapso de su gobierno central. Esto provocó una guerra civil, desplazamientos masivos y crisis repetidas como sequías e inundaciones.

**Qué pasó** – El 31 de octubre, las Naciones Unidas finalizaron su misión política en Somalia, llamada UNTMIS, después de casi 30 años ayudando al país a reconstruirse. El Representante Especial Adjunto de la ONU, Raisedon Zenenga, dijo que esta decisión llega tras avances reales en la creación de instituciones gubernamentales y procesos políticos.

**Impacto** – El cierre de la misión UNTMIS significa que el gobierno somalí ahora lidera por completo sus esfuerzos de recuperación. Se han logrado mejoras importantes en la formación de gobiernos nacionales y regionales, protección de derechos humanos y participación política. A la vez, agencias de la ONU continúan apoyando proyectos de salud, educación, alimentación y seguridad, como nuevos puestos de mercado para mujeres y programas de comidas escolares.

**Próximo paso** – Somalia enfrenta retos como la pobreza, una economía frágil y amenazas de seguridad de grupos como Al-Shabaab. La comunidad internacional seguirá apoyando a Somalia con ayuda humanitaria y programas de desarrollo. Los líderes somalíes trabajarán para fortalecer su economía y mantener la paz.

**Resumen en una frase** – Tras décadas de apoyo político de la ONU, Somalia asume el control de su futuro mientras sigue recibiendo ayuda internacional clave para un progreso duradero.
